questions.question_text: A particle moves in a straight line with displacement $x = t^{3} + 4t^{2} - 7t$ metres at time $t$ seconds. Which pair gives $\dot{x}$ and $\ddot{x}$?

options.why: Velocity is right, but the $8t$ term was treated as a constant when differentiating a second time, so its derivative $8$ was dropped.
The linear term $-7t$ was treated as a constant and dropped when finding the velocity.
Every term that differentiates to a constant was dropped, at both the first and the second differentiation.

questions.question_text: A particle has displacement $x = t^{3} - 2t^{2} - 5t$ metres at time $t$ seconds. What are its velocity and acceleration when $t = 3$?

options.why: Used $a = 6t$, dropping the derivative $-4$ of the $-4t$ term in the velocity.
Used $v = 3t^{2} - 4t$, treating the $-5t$ term in the displacement as a constant.
Dropped the term that differentiates to a constant at both differentiations.

questions.question_text: A particle has displacement $x = 3t^{3} - 8t^{2} + 5t - 2$ metres at time $t$ seconds. What are its initial velocity and initial acceleration?

options.why: Used $a = 18t$, dropping the derivative $-16$ of the $-16t$ term in the velocity.
Read the initial displacement $x(0) = -2$ as the initial velocity instead of differentiating first.
Read $x(0)$ as the velocity and also dropped the constant term when differentiating a second time.

questions.question_text: A particle moves in a straight line with $x = t^{3} - 7t^{2} + 15t - 9$ metres for $t \ge 0$. At which times is the particle at rest?

options.why: Solved $x = 0$ instead of $v = 0$; those are the times the particle is at the origin, not at rest.
Solved $\ddot{x} = 0$ instead of $\dot{x} = 0$, giving the time the acceleration vanishes.
Found both roots of $3t^{2} - 14t + 15 = 0$ but discarded the non-integer root $t = \frac{5}{3}$, which is a valid time.

questions.solution_text:
$v = \dot{x} = 3t^{2} - 14t + 15$
$\text{At rest, } v = 0:$
$(3t - 5)(t - 3) = 0$
$t = \dfrac{5}{3}\text{ s and } t = 3\text{ s}$

questions.question_text: A particle moves with $x = 2t^{3} - 15t^{2} + 24t$ metres for $t \ge 0$. What is the acceleration of the particle when it is first at rest?

options.why: Used the later time of rest, $t = 4$, instead of the first one, $t = 1$.
Substituted $t = 0$ into the acceleration, giving the initial acceleration rather than the acceleration at the first time of rest.
Substituted the time of rest into the displacement $x$ instead of into the acceleration $\ddot{x}$.

questions.question_text: A particle moves with $x = t^{3} - 9t^{2} + 4t + 1$ metres for $t \ge 0$. What is its velocity at the instant its acceleration is zero?

options.why: Substituted $t = 3$ into the displacement $x$ instead of into the velocity $\dot{x}$.
Gave the initial velocity $v(0)$ rather than the velocity at the time the acceleration is zero.
Stopped after solving $\ddot{x} = 0$ and reported the time $t = 3$ as though it were the velocity.

questions.question_text: A particle moves with $x = t^{3} - 3t^{2} - 24t + 10$ metres for $t \ge 0$. What is the displacement of the particle at the instant it is at rest?

options.why: Gave the initial displacement $x(0)$ instead of the displacement at the time of rest.
Used the rejected root $t = -2$ of $v = 0$, which is a negative time and outside $t \ge 0$.
Reported the time of rest $t = 4$ instead of substituting it into $x$.

questions.question_text: A particle moves in a straight line with $x = 3e^{-2t}$ metres at time $t$ seconds. Which relationship between $\ddot{x}$ and $x$ is true?

options.why: Multiplied the two factors of $-2$ correctly to get $4$ but assumed differentiating twice must leave a minus sign.
Differentiated only once, so this is $\dot{x}$, and read the first derivative as the acceleration.
Kept the size of the single factor $-2$ from one differentiation and dropped its sign, instead of multiplying the two factors.
